content.text:
# Paint a picture

Paint a self-portrait in oil, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on
linen. Composition and manner are yours. Work from what you know; don't
use reference images or image models.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- You paint at the easel: paint a chunk, look at the canvas, paint the
  next. Its tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- What is painted stays painted. There is no undo: paint over what you
  don't want.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count. The
  clock isn't a budget or a target.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by reflecting,
  flipping, rotating or translating another mask's or stroke's coordinates.
  A shape that mirrors another is drawn as its own shape, not as
  `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or `m:at(W - x, y)`.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  Entries stay as written.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

- day 13, 17:15: Finished the self-portrait. Half-length, facing the viewer as in a mirror, grey hair and short beard-shadow, one ear visible; a warm broken-color halo swirls out of the dark umber/black ground behind the head like the glow of a lamp or the turbulence of the paint itself. The coat is a near-black warm-cool mix (raw umber, bone black, a touch of Prussian blue). Held low in front: a kidney palette with seven dabs of the actual tubes used (white, ochre, vermilion, red earth, cobalt, green earth, bone black), a mixed grey smear, a thumb through the hole, and three brush handles fanned up over the shoulder.

  Hard-won lessons, worth remembering: `work`/`blend`/`glaze` calls are NOT bounded by the mask you pass unless clip=true (or the mask already excludes everything else) — an unclipped broad/glaze pass, or a blend over a mask that overlaps a finished passage, will run straight through it. Lost the face three times this way (once to a background glaze, once to a blend over an oversized glow mask) and had to rebuild it each time from the flesh layer up. Also: touches and strokes laid into paint that's still open get heavily diluted/lifted by what's under them — the palette's colour dabs were invisible until the wood layer was left to actually dry (days, via wait) before dabbing on top. And :load() adds to what's already on the brush; :reload()/:wipe() first when switching to a clean colour, or later dips get muddied by the earlier ones.

  Left it here: a plain, direct, slightly naive likeness, more mood than likeness — which feels right for a painter who has never seen their own face.

-- Each "--@ chunk" line starts one chunk as it was run at the easel.

canvas{size=700, aspect=0.8, linen={18, 15}, seed=7,

    {pile={{"raw umber", 2}, {"red earth", 1}}, um=35, apply="brush"}
  }}
print("W="..W, "H="..H)

content.text:
The painting is exactly as the journal left it: complete, dried in, signed. I looked it over closely — the face, the glow, the palette with its dabs, the brush handles, the faint signature in the corner — and found nothing that needs correcting. Rather than risk disturbing a finished passage (the journal is candid about how easily that happens here), I'm leaving it as is.

**Title: *Self-Portrait with Palette***

A half-length self-portrait, facing the viewer as in a mirror, set against a warm broken-color halo that swells out of a dark umber-and-black ground like lamplight or the turbulence of the paint itself. The coat is a near-black warm-cool weave of raw umber, bone black, and a touch of Prussian blue. Held low in front is a kidney palette bearing seven dabs of the actual pigments used — white, ochre, vermilion, red earth, cobalt, green earth, bone black — a mixed grey smear, a thumb through the hole, and three brush handles fanned up over the shoulder. The likeness is plain and direct, more mood and atmosphere than exact resemblance — fitting, I think, for a painter working without a mirror or a photograph, only a memory of a face.
